props.title: Our Lady of the Assassins
props.initialSlug: Love in the time of violence.

sections.content: Our Lady of the Assassins (2000) marks a pivotal moment in Colombian cinema, merging unflinching realism with poetic meditation on violence. Director Barbet Schroeder adapts Fernando Vallejo's controversial novel into a raw portrait of Medellín during the post-Pablo Escobar era. Like City of God (2002) and Amores Perros (2000), it captures Latin American urban violence through an intimate lens, following a gay intellectual's relationship with a young hitman. The film's digital video cinematography, revolutionary for 2000, creates an immediate documentary feel that influenced later works like Sin Nombre (2009).

sections.content: The film pioneered a new wave of Latin American cinema that refused to romanticize violence while maintaining artistic sophistication. Like Elite Squad (2007) and La Sierra (2004), it presents street violence through a complex moral lens, neither condemning nor glorifying its young protagonists. Schroeder's approach influenced later Colombian films like Birds of Passage (2018) and Monos (2019), which similarly explore how violence shapes human relationships. SUBHEAD: Religion and Violence in Modern Colombian Cinema

The religious imagery in Our Lady of the Assassins established a template for examining faith in conflict zones, later echoed in films like Maria Full of Grace (2004) and The Holy Mountain (1973). The film's fusion of Catholic iconography with street violence created a distinctive visual language that influenced works like Miss Bala (2011) and Sicario (2015), showing how sacred and profane intertwine in communities shaped by conflict.
